what_its_for: Ondansetron helps prevent and treat nausea and vomiting. It is commonly used to prevent nausea caused by chemotherapy, radiation therapy, or surgery. It works by blocking signals in your brain that trigger the urge to vomit.
how_to_take: Take ondansetron exactly as your doctor tells you. It comes in several forms: a regular tablet you swallow with water, a dissolvable tablet (ODT) that melts on your tongue without water, or an oral film strip that dissolves in your mouth. For the dissolvable tablet or film strip, do not chew it — just place it on your tongue and let it dissolve completely. You can take ondansetron with or without food. Do not take more than your prescribed dose.
dosing: Your dose depends on what you are being treated for and your age. A common adult dose is 4 mg to 8 mg taken every 8 hours as needed, or as directed by your doctor. For surgery-related nausea, you may take a single dose before or after a procedure. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions, as doses vary widely. Do not take more than 32 mg in one day.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose and you are taking ondansetron on a regular schedule, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do not take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. If you are taking ondansetron only when needed for nausea, take it as soon as you feel sick.
storage: Store ondansetron tablets and dissolvable strips at room temperature, between 59°F and 86°F (15°C to 30°C). Keep the dissolvable tablets and film strips in their original sealed packaging until you are ready to use them. Keep all medications away from heat, moisture, and direct sunlight. Do not store in the bathroom. Keep out of reach of children and pets.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol while taking ondansetron, as it can increase drowsiness and dizziness. Be careful driving or operating heavy machinery until you know how this medication affects you. Tell your doctor about all other medications you take, especially apomorphine, as combining these can cause a dangerous drop in blood pressure. Avoid taking medications that affect your heart rhythm without checking with your doctor first.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or get emergency help if you experience: an irregular or fast heartbeat or pounding in your chest; severe dizziness or fainting; sudden changes in vision; difficulty breathing; swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat (signs of an allergic reaction); severe headache; muscle stiffness, twitching, or uncontrolled movements; or if your nausea and vomiting do not improve or get worse. Also call your doctor if you develop a rash or hives.
when_it_works: Ondansetron usually starts working within 30 minutes after you take it. It works best when taken before nausea starts — for example, before chemotherapy or surgery. The effects typically last 4 to 8 hours. If your nausea is not controlled after taking the medication, contact your doctor rather than taking extra doses.
special_populations: Older adults and people with liver disease may need a lower dose, as the medication can build up in the body more easily. Pregnant women should talk to their doctor before using ondansetron, especially during the first trimester, as there may be a small risk to the baby. Breastfeeding mothers should also consult their doctor before use. Children's doses are based on body weight and age, so always follow your child's doctor's instructions carefully.
